werk/frank-boeijen-groep-zwart-wit.text: On 21 August 1983, fifteen-year-old Kerwin Duinmeijer was stabbed to death in Amsterdam because he was Black. Frank Boeijen wrote Zwart wit about it, and it became a hit in 1984. It is new wave in Dutch, with cool guitars and synthesizers. Boeijen showed that a pop song in one's own language could also be about a racist murder in one's own country.
werk/frank-boeijen-groep-zwart-wit.listen: Listen to the cool guitars and the detached vocals beneath a lyric that asks how something like this could happen.

werk/frank-sinatra-in-the-wee-small-hour.text:
In the early 1950s, Frank Sinatra's career seemed to have passed its peak. After his comeback at Capitol and an Oscar for From Here to Eternity, he recorded this album in 1955, while his marriage to Ava Gardner was falling apart. Nelson Riddle wrote the arrangements and Voyle Gilmore produced. The sessions in Hollywood began at eight in the evening and ran past midnight. He chose the songs carefully and decided the running order himself.

The songs deal with melancholy, lost love and nightlife, which is why the album is sometimes called one of the first concept albums. Much of the accompaniment is sparse, without brass or strings. Dancing on the Ceiling and Glad to Be Unhappy were given a small jazz line-up, and Mood Indigo and Ill Wind are the most jazz-flavoured pieces. The record reached number two on the Billboard 200 and helped to make the 12-inch LP popular in pop music.
werk/frank-sinatra-in-the-wee-small-hour.listen: In Can't We Be Friends?, listen to the opening: a few chords on a minimalist guitar, still without orchestra, and then the voice moving from calm to overconfident.

werk/frank-sinatra-songs-for-swingin-lov.text:
After the sombre In the Wee Small Hours of 1955, Frank Sinatra chose a very different tone. His tenth studio album, and his fourth for Capitol, was released in March 1956 and, like the previous records, was arranged by Nelson Riddle. Existing pop standards sounded hipper and jazzier here, full of exuberance. A slow ballad, Memories of You, was recorded but left off because it did not suit an album of swinging, bright numbers.

It became the first record to top the new British albums chart, which appeared for the first time on 22 July 1956. In 2000 it was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame. Many fans rank it as his best or second-best album. The magazine Uncut later wrote that in its own day it was an answer to the rising tide of rock 'n' roll, with the rhythmic sound of Riddle's orchestra.
werk/frank-sinatra-songs-for-swingin-lov.listen: In I've Got You Under My Skin, listen to the rhythmic drive of the orchestra beneath the vocals, which makes an old standard suddenly sound thoroughly contemporary.

werk/frank-sinatra-songs-for-young-lover.text:
Songs for Young Lovers was Frank Sinatra's first album for Capitol Records, released in January 1954. It is his seventh studio album. In the nightclubs of Las Vegas he had developed a more mature, jazzier sound, and with producer Voyle Gilmore he recorded the arrangements he had sung at the Riviera and the Sands. Nelson Riddle conducted the sessions, the beginning of a twenty-year collaboration. Almost all of the arrangements were by George Siravo.

The album consists of eight standards built around a single theme, including My Funny Valentine, A Foggy Day and I Get a Kick Out of You. It was also the singer's first album not to be issued as a 78 rpm album set. In 2002 it was added to the Library of Congress's National Recording Registry.
werk/frank-sinatra-songs-for-young-lover.listen: Listen to My Funny Valentine and notice how intimate the voice sounds, with only eleven musicians around him.

werk/frank-sinatra-swing-easy.text:
Swing Easy! is Frank Sinatra's eighth studio album, released in 1954 on Capitol. It was his second record for the label and the first with arrangements by Nelson Riddle, who had only conducted on Songs for Young Lovers. Because only about fourteen minutes fitted on each side of a ten-inch record, the album contains eight songs.

As the title suggests, it is about bright, light-touch swingers. All the songs were standards, such as Just One of Those Things, Wrap Your Troubles in Dreams and All of Me. He felt that they benefited from the new theme, the new arrangements and his increasingly playful, layered singing. In 1955 the eight songs were combined with Songs for Young Lovers on a sixteen-track LP. In 2000 the record was placed at number 368 in Colin Larkin's list.
werk/frank-sinatra-swing-easy.listen: Listen to All of Me and notice the playful way the singer phrases the melody.

werk/frank-zappa-apostrophe.text:
Apostrophe (’) was released in March 1974 and followed the successful Over-Nite Sensation. Both albums were made with the same musicians. The first side and Over-Nite Sensation itself were recorded together in the spring of 1973. The second side comes from various sessions in 1972, with overdubs from 1973 and 1974. The drums on Excentrifugal Forz date back as far as 1969. Like many Frank Zappa albums, it is a mixture of archive material and new work.

Don't Eat the Yellow Snow and Nanook Rubs It tell of a dream in which the singer sees himself as an Eskimo called Nanook. The story continues in St. Alfonzo's Pancake Breakfast. Apostrophe' is an instrumental jam with a heavily distorted bass part by Jack Bruce of Cream. Uncle Remus is about racism. The edited version of Don't Eat the Yellow Snow was a hit in the Billboard Top 100, and the album became the greatest commercial success of his career.
werk/frank-zappa-apostrophe.listen: In Apostrophe', listen to Jack Bruce's heavily distorted bass and the jazz-rock interplay in this instrumental piece.

werk/frank-zappa-chunga-s-revenge.text:
Chunga's Revenge was released on 23 October 1970 on Bizarre, Frank Zappa's own label, and distributed by Reprise. It is his third solo album and the first on which Mark Volman and Howard Kaylan play, two former members of the Turtles who became known as Flo & Eddie. The recordings ran from July 1969 to August 1970 and took place in various studios in the United States and London. Twenty Small Cigars comes from the Hot Rats sessions of 1969.

The material is eclectic: a guitar jam, a bluesy number, a jazz interlude and an avant-garde live improvisation. The Clap is a short percussion piece on which Zappa is the only musician. The vocal numbers are about sex and groupies. A French reviewer praised the versatile guitarist with his wah-wah pedal. The writer Ben Watson heard Zappa's most Oriental-sounding guitar in Transylvania Boogie.
werk/frank-zappa-chunga-s-revenge.listen: Listen to Transylvania Boogie and notice the guitar solo with wah-wah pedal, which according to one Zappa expert sounds strikingly Oriental.

werk/frank-zappa-hot-rats.text:
In the summer of 1969, Frank Zappa began work on his second solo album, while already thinking of disbanding his group, the Mothers of Invention. That happened in August. Only the multi-instrumentalist Ian Underwood played on it as a Mother. The others included the bassist Shuggie Otis, who was fifteen at the time, and the violinists Don Sugarcane Harris and Jean-Luc Ponty.

It was recorded on a home-built 16-track recorder in Hollywood. Thanks to overdubs, a handful of musicians sound like a large ensemble, and for the first time in rock the drums were given a stereo sound. Five of the six pieces are instrumental, jazz-inspired and full of solos, very different from his earlier satirical records. Only Willie The Pimp has vocals, by Captain Beefheart. Zappa himself called the album a movie for your ears. It is dedicated to his newborn son Dweezil.
werk/frank-zappa-hot-rats.listen: In Peaches En Regalia, listen to how few musicians it takes to make a rich, full sound, and to how the melody keeps returning throughout the piece.

werk/frank-zappa-one-size-fits-all.text:
One Size Fits All, from June 1975, is Frank Zappa's twentieth album and the last studio album by the Mothers of Invention. It was released on his own label DiscReet and followed Apostrophe, his highest-charting album in the United States. The record was made with the line-up of the Mothers from the summer and autumn of 1974: George Duke on keyboards and vocals, Chester Thompson on drums, Ruth Underwood on marimba and percussion, Tom Fowler on bass and Napoleon Murphy Brock on saxophone, flute and vocals. On Can't Afford No Shoes the bassist is James Youmans, because Fowler had broken his hand on tour. Captain Beefheart plays harmonica under a pseudonym.

He was very proud of the album and complained about the lack of promotion by the distributor, Warner Bros. Records. The cover shows a large sofa. According to a reviewer at AllMusic, it is an essential album from the band's third period.
werk/frank-zappa-one-size-fits-all.listen: In Inca Roads, listen to how the band makes a rich, many-coloured sound with marimba and keyboards.

werk/frank-zappa-waka-jawaka.text:
Waka/Jawaka was released in July 1972 and is Frank Zappa's fourth solo album. It is a jazz-inspired successor to Hot Rats of 1969 and the precursor of The Grand Wazoo, which followed in November 1972. According to Zappa, the title once came up on a Ouija board. The four pieces feature, among others, the trumpeter Sal Marquez, the drummer Aynsley Dunbar and the keyboard player George Duke.

Big Swifty is jazz fusion with plenty of brass, room for improvisation and changing time signatures. It Just Might Be a One-Shot Deal tells a strange story about hallucinations, sung by Marquez and Janet Ferguson, with a dreamy pedal steel by Sneaky Pete Kleinow. The first reviews were mixed. Rolling Stone called it second-rate Miles Davis, but still one of Zappa's most enjoyable records. Its reputation has grown since.
werk/frank-zappa-waka-jawaka.listen: Listen to Big Swifty and notice Sal Marquez's many trumpets and the changing time signatures before the piece settles into a swinging rhythm.

werk/freddie-hubbard-goin-up.text:
Goin' Up was released in 1961 on Blue Note. Freddie Hubbard plays on it with Hank Mobley on tenor saxophone, McCoy Tyner on piano, Paul Chambers on bass and Philly Joe Jones on drums. It is a quintet in the classic hard bop line-up of the day.

The six pieces come from various composers. Kenny Dorham wrote Asiatic Rates and Karioka, Mobley The Changing Scene and A Peck a Sec, and the trumpeter himself Blues for Brenda. I Wished I Knew is by Bill Smith. Scott Yanow of AllMusic praised his excellent solos. It is a record that is above all about the interplay and the solos of this group of five.
werk/freddie-hubbard-goin-up.listen: Listen to Blues for Brenda, the trumpeter's own piece, and notice his trumpet solo.

werk/freddie-hubbard-hub-cap.text:
Hub Cap was released in 1961 on Blue Note. Freddie Hubbard plays here with the trombonist Julian Priester, the tenor saxophonist Jimmy Heath, the pianist Cedar Walton, the bassist Larry Ridley and the drummer Philly Joe Jones. The title refers to his nickname.

The album contains two pieces by others: Cry Me Not, written by Randy Weston for this session and arranged by Melba Liston, and Plexus by Walton. The trumpeter called Cry Me Not the most interesting piece on the record. He dedicates Luana to his cousin, and Earmon Jr. is named after his brother, a pianist. The British critic John Fordham wrote in The Guardian in 2003 that the music throws you back to a time when the muscular dynamics of hard bop were still commercially popular. Fordham praised the opening solo on the title track and the warmth of Cry Me Not.
werk/freddie-hubbard-hub-cap.listen: In Hub Cap, listen to the opening trumpet solo. Notice how fierce and sharp the tone is and how fast he plays.

werk/freddie-hubbard-open-sesame.text:
Open Sesame was the debut of the then 22-year-old trumpeter Freddie Hubbard. He recorded it on 19 June 1960 in Rudy Van Gelder's studio in Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey, for the Blue Note label. Playing with him were Tina Brooks on tenor saxophone, McCoy Tyner on piano, Sam Jones on bass and Clifford Jarvis on drums. Brooks wrote the title song and Gypsy Blue.

The repertoire combines original work with standards such as But Beautiful and All or Nothing at All. A reviewer at DownBeat praised the youthful vigour and fierceness of the debutant and saw in it a good sign for the small jazz combo. The Penguin Guide to Jazz included the record in its Core Collection and called it a great Blue Note set.
werk/freddie-hubbard-open-sesame.listen: Listen to Open Sesame and notice how trumpet and tenor saxophone play Brooks's theme.

werk/froukje-groter-dan-ik.text: In 2021, Froukje Veenstra broke through with electropop in Dutch. Groter dan ik is about climate anxiety: the feeling that the world's problems are too big for one person. Set it beside Welterusten mijnheer de president: Boudewijn de Groot sang about Vietnam in 1966, while Froukje sings about the future of the planet. Both in their own language, for an audience of their own age.
werk/froukje-groter-dan-ik.listen: Listen to the electronic beat and the soft voice beneath a lyric about something too big to carry.

werk/funkadelic-america-eats-its-young.text:
In May 1972 came Funkadelic's fourth studio album, and immediately their first double album. For the first time all the House Guests took part, among them Bootsy Collins, Catfish Collins, Chicken Gunnels, Rob McCollough and Kash Waddy, and on most tracks also the band U.S. with Garry Shider and Cordell Mosson. Unlike the earlier records, it was recorded in Toronto and in the United Kingdom.

The album is above all experimental, contains no hits and reads like a lesson in the history of Black music. The biographer Kris Needs called it George Clinton's great statement on the Vietnam War. Reviews were divided. Robert Christgau liked only Biological Speculation and Loose Booty and later called it the group's worst album. Ned Raggett of AllMusic thought it worth every minute. According to the Rolling Stone Album Guide, it contains elements that led Clinton to Parliament, such as vocal harmonies and the playful humour of Bernie Worrell.
werk/funkadelic-america-eats-its-young.listen: Listen to Everybody Is Going to Make It This Time, recorded in London with the help of the drummer Ginger Baker, and notice the drumming.

werk/funkadelic-cosmic-slop.text:
Cosmic Slop was released on 9 July 1973 on Westbound Records. It was Funkadelic's fifth studio album. It was a commercial failure, with no single in the charts, and reached number 112 on the pop chart and number 21 on the R&B chart. Only long after its release did critics rate it more highly. It was the first album with a sleeve and liner notes by Pedro Bell, who continued to do so until the end of the band. The guitarist Eddie Hazel, who had left a year earlier, no longer plays on it.

Bernie Worrell plays keyboards, melodica and the strings on This Broken Heart, which Ben Edwards sings. Garry Shider and Ron Bykowski play guitar. You Can't Miss What You Can't Measure reworks the Parliaments single Heart Trouble from 1965. The title track, with Shider as singer, was later often remade by new line-ups. Lloyd Bradley wrote in Q that the album is a link between frighteningly dark musings and outright weirdness.
werk/funkadelic-cosmic-slop.listen: Listen to Cosmic Slop, with Garry Shider as singer, and notice the two guitars of Shider and Ron Bykowski.

werk/funkadelic-free-your-mind-and-your-.text:
Free Your Mind… and Your Ass Will Follow is Funkadelic's second studio album and was released on 20 July 1970 on Westbound Records. The band recorded it in Detroit, at United Sound Studios, Audio Graphic Services and G-M Recording Studios. George Clinton said he wanted to see whether they could record an entire album with everyone on LSD.

The title song is full of feedback and takes up a third of the running time. The piece describes a mystical road to redemption: free your mind, and the rest will follow. Several other songs, including Eulogy and Light, play with Christian texts such as the Lord's Prayer and Psalm 23 and mock capitalism. The record reached number 92 on the American pop chart, and I Wanna Know If It's Good to You? became a single. Critics were divided. Robert Christgau thought Funky Dollar Bill the most successful, while AllMusic praised the record as an album of songs ranging from good to stunningly good.
werk/funkadelic-free-your-mind-and-your-.listen: Listen to the title track and notice the feedback and the distorted guitar and bass. The piece takes up a third of the entire record.

werk/funkadelic-maggot-brain.text:
Maggot Brain was released in July 1971 on Westbound Records. George Clinton produced the album, which was recorded in late 1970 and early 1971 at United Sound Systems in Detroit. It was the last album by the original line-up: afterwards the guitarist Tawl Ross, the bassist Billy Nelson and the drummer Tiki Fulwood left, and only Clinton, the guitarist Eddie Hazel and the keyboard player Bernie Worrell remained.

The album opens with a spoken passage by Clinton and the ten-minute title track, largely an improvised solo by Hazel. According to legend, Clinton asked him to play as if he had just heard that his mother was dead. Hazel used fuzz and wah, inspired by Jimi Hendrix, and Clinton added echo. The rest of the album offers funk, blues and gospel, and the closer Wars of Armageddon is a long freak-out. The first reviews were divided. Later, critics called it one of the darkest and most intense records ever.
werk/funkadelic-maggot-brain.listen: Listen to the title track and notice how Hazel's guitar gains more and more room while the rest of the band stays in the background.

werk/funkadelic-one-nation-under-a-groov.text:
One Nation Under a Groove is Funkadelic's tenth studio album, the rock-oriented sister project of George Clinton's funk collective. It was released in September 1978 on Warner Bros. The recording took place at United Sound Studio in Detroit. One track was recorded live at the Monroe Civic Center in Louisiana. It was the first record on which the keyboard player and songwriter Walter Junie Morrison took part.

According to one academic, the music draws on progressive rock, progressive soul, Hendrix and Sly Stone. Critics heard distorted guitar riffs in the style of Hendrix, even where the music was meant for the dance floor. The album became the group's most commercially successful: it was number 1 on the R&B chart and went platinum. It is regarded as the finest realisation of Funkadelic's ambitions and as a source of ideas for later rock and rap.
werk/funkadelic-one-nation-under-a-groov.listen: In the title track, One Nation Under a Groove, listen to how the group sings together like a choir, on top of a tight, danceable groove.

werk/gang-of-four-entertainment.text:
Gang of Four's debut album was released in September 1979 on EMI, and in North America on Warner Bros. It is built on punk, with influences from funk, reggae and dub. The singer Jon King and the guitarist Andy Gill produced it together with their manager Rob Warr. The lyrics, influenced by Situationism, feminism and Marx, are about consumption, working life and the way the media colour reality. The starting point is that the personal is political. The sleeve shows a Native American and a cowboy shaking hands, with a caption that exposes the appearance of friendship.

At Home He's a Tourist reached number 58 in the British charts. For Top of the Pops a word in the lyrics had to be changed, but the band refused and the appearance did not take place. Critics called the record a pillar of post-punk. NME placed it at number five in its list for 1979.
werk/gang-of-four-entertainment.listen: Listen to At Home He's a Tourist. Notice the sharp guitar and what the lyrics say about the life of the worker.

werk/gang-of-four-hard.text:
Hard is the fourth studio album by this English post-punk group and was released in 1983 on Warner Bros. It was the first album without the drummer Hugo Burnham; the bassist Dave Allen had already left before the previous album, Songs of the Free. Jon King and Andy Gill remained, with Sara Lee on bass and guest musicians for strings, brass and backing vocals.

The sound shifted from a hard, stomping dance rhythm to a smoother, more heavily arranged pop sound. The New York Times wrote that the band had swapped its sharp dance rock for something closer to traditional disco. For some fans that was a step too far.
werk/gang-of-four-hard.listen: Listen to Is It Love and notice the polished production and the backing vocals: how much of the hard post-punk sound is left?

werk/gang-of-four-mall.text:
Seven years after the group broke up, the founders Jon King and Andy Gill came together again for Mall, the fifth album, from 1991. It sounds smoothly produced, with plenty of synthesizers and imitation funk rhythms. Gail Ann Dorsey plays bass, and a succession of drummers and backing singers contribute.

The lyrics take the band back to politics. As the title suggests, they keep returning to consumption and the economy. F.M.U.S.A. is an essay on the Vietnam War, built from many samples. Soul Rebel is a cover of the song by Bob Marley and the Wailers. Rolling Stone thought it an adventurous, often compelling album that courts commercial success and yet indicts American consumer culture.
werk/gang-of-four-mall.listen: Listen to F.M.U.S.A. and notice the samples: which sounds do you hear in it, and how do they fit the subject, the war in Vietnam?

werk/gang-of-four-solid-gold.text:
Solid Gold is the second album by the British post-punk band Gang of Four and was released in 1981. Two songs, Outside the Trains Don't Run on Time and He'd Send in the Army, are re-recordings of songs that had previously appeared on a British single. The line-up consisted of Andy Gill on guitar, Jon King on vocals, Dave Allen on bass and Hugo Burnham on drums.

The guitar sounds scratchy and feverish and breaks through the mix at key moments. The lyrics are about the personal politics of consumption and desire, as in What We All Want, and about broader issues such as American culture in Cheeseburger and Thatcher's policies. The album was well received, although many critics found it less consistent than the debut, Entertainment!. Pitchfork placed it at number 24 among the best records of the 1980s. Uncut called it their best.
werk/gang-of-four-solid-gold.listen: Listen to What We All Want and notice the sharp, feverish guitar and what the lyrics are about.

werk/gang-of-four-songs-of-the-free.text:
Songs of the Free is Gang of Four's third studio album and was released in 1982. It is the first record with Sara Lee on bass, succeeding Dave Allen. Andy Gill and Jon King wrote all the songs at Mount Pleasant Studios in London. Besides Gill, King and Lee, the drummer Hugo Burnham played, and Stevie Lange and Joy Yates sang backing vocals.

The sound moves towards R&B and funk, and gives up some of the sharper edges of earlier records. Call Me Up opens the record, with I Love a Man in a Uniform following. Later reissues added bonus tracks and a slightly altered running order, until EMI restored the original order in 2008. In 2015 a limited edition appeared on coloured vinyl. Pitchfork placed the album at number 99 of the 1980s.
werk/gang-of-four-songs-of-the-free.listen: Listen to Call Me Up and notice how the rhythm moves more towards funk than on the earlier records.

werk/gary-burton-new-vibe-man-in-town.text:
This is the debut of the vibraphonist Gary Burton as a bandleader. He recorded it in 1961 for the RCA label, in Studio B of RCA Victor in New York, on 6 and 7 July. Burton plays in a trio with the bassist Gene Cherico and the drummer Joe Morello, who was known from Dave Brubeck's band.

The programme consists of eight pieces. It includes jazz standards such as Over the Rainbow, Like Someone in Love and You Stepped Out of a Dream, alongside Joy Spring by Clifford Brown and Sir John by Blue Mitchell. Minor Blues, Our Waltz and So Many Things have also found a place. In this way the album sketches the picture of a bebop-minded player who already sounds mature on the vibraphone. The AllMusic reviewer wrote that the record shows he was a brilliant player from the very start of his career.
werk/gary-burton-new-vibe-man-in-town.listen: Listen to Joy Spring and notice how the vibraphone plays the theme with only bass and drums alongside. Hear how few instruments are needed to carry the piece.

werk/gary-burton-something-s-coming.text:
The album was recorded in August 1963 in Studio B of RCA Victor in New York and was released a year later on RCA. It was the third album that the vibraphonist Gary Burton made as a leader. He plays here with the guitarist Jim Hall, the bassist Chuck Israels and the drummer Larry Bunker, three musicians associated with the pianist Bill Evans.

The seven pieces consist of standards such as On Green Dolphin Street, Little Girl Blue and Summertime, supplemented by pieces by Michael Gibbs, a number by Jim Hall and the title song from West Side Story, written by Leonard Bernstein and Stephen Sondheim. The critic Scott Yanow wrote on Allmusic that the vibraphonist was rapidly developing into a fresh new voice on his instrument.
werk/gary-burton-something-s-coming.listen: Listen to On Green Dolphin Street and notice how vibraphone, guitar, bass and drums play together like a small group.

werk/gary-burton-the-groovy-sound-of-mus.text:
RCA made this album because the label had promised the composer Richard Rodgers that artists from its own catalogue would record songs from The Sound of Music, during the negotiations over the 1965 film soundtrack. There were two sessions in New York in December 1964. At the first, the vibraphonist Gary Burton played in a jazz sextet, and also played Edelweiss solo. The second featured a small orchestra under the direction of Gary McFarland, who also arranged.

The vibraphonist was unhappy with it later. He found McFarland's arrangements conventional and uninspiring and was embarrassed by the title and the sleeve. After his complaint and the threat of leaving the label, he was given more say. The reviewer Ken Dryden, on the other hand, found the album a treat, because jazz musicians had done little with this musical, apart from My Favorite Things.
werk/gary-burton-the-groovy-sound-of-mus.listen: Listen to Edelweiss, which the vibraphonist plays without a band, and notice how the vibraphone carries the melody alone.

werk/gary-burton-who-is-gary-burton.text:
This album by the vibraphonist Gary Burton was recorded in September 1962 in Studio A of RCA Victor in New York and was released on RCA. The line-up is larger than on his debut. You hear, among others, the alto saxophonist Phil Woods, the trombonist Bob Brookmeyer, the trumpeter Clark Terry, the pianist Tommy Flanagan, the bassist John Neves and the drummer Joe Morello. Two pieces were recorded on the first day, the other five a day later.

The pieces, too, are varied. There are works by Chris Swansen, Michael Gibbs, George Shearing and Jaki Byard, alongside My Funny Valentine by Lorenz Hart and Richard Rodgers. According to AllMusic, the young vibraphonist had already proved himself as an accompanist and was now breaking new ground as a master of his instrument. He played with four mallets at once, seemingly with little effort.
werk/gary-burton-who-is-gary-burton.listen: Listen to My Funny Valentine and notice the tone of the vibraphone. Try to hear how the melody and the chords sound at the same time.

werk/gary-numan-dance.text:
Dance was released on 4 September 1981 on Beggars Banquet. It was Gary Numan's third solo album and his first studio record after the farewell concerts at Wembley Arena. He had been working on it since late 1980 and was deliberately looking for new directions. With sparse electronic sounds, drum machines and plenty of percussion, it became his most experimental album to date. Mick Karn, the bassist of Japan, played on it and improvised a saxophone riff on She's Got Claws, of which the first take was kept. The violinist Nash the Slash and Queen's drummer Roger Taylor also took part.

The single She's Got Claws reached number 6 and the album number 3. The reviews were mixed: some praised the less commercial course, others reacted sceptically. Later The Quietus called the record one of his most interesting albums, with the ten-minute Cry, The Clock Said as its highlight.
werk/gary-numan-dance.listen: Listen to Cry, The Clock Said and notice the steady beats, the softly glittering keyboards and the violinist Nash the Slash, who gives the piece a mournful tone.

werk/gary-numan-i-assassin.text:
I, Assassin was released on 10 September 1982 on Beggars Banquet and is Gary Numan's fourth solo album. It came after Dance of 1981. He wrote and recorded most of it between January and March 1982, after a trip around the world in a small aeroplane. That trip, during which he also nearly crashed, gave him, by his own account, more self-confidence.

A major role was played by the bassist Pino Palladino, who played fretless. He brought the bass lines to the foreground, so that the fretless bass served as a lead melody for the first time. The sound is strongly rhythmic. Music for Chameleons and an American remix of White Boys and Heroes unexpectedly became popular in American clubs. Three singles reached the British top twenty, We Take Mystery among them at number nine. The British music press was negative. The album reached number eight.
werk/gary-numan-i-assassin.listen: Listen to Music for Chameleons and notice Pino Palladino's fretless bass, which carries the melody here.

werk/gary-numan-telekon.text:
Telekon is Gary Numan's second solo album and entered the British albums chart at number 1 in September 1980. It closes the machine phase that he had begun with Replicas and The Pleasure Principle. The recording was almost finished by December 1979, but the contract with Beggars Banquet allowed only one album a year, so the release had to wait.

The sound is richer than on the previous record: plenty of guitars, a greater variety of synthesizers and, in addition, viola and violin. Pieces such as I'm an Agent and The Joy Circuit sound heavy, while Sleep by Windows and Remember I Was Vapour are wistful. On several tracks a note of farewell can be heard, which suited his decision, soon afterwards, to stop playing live. The British press was largely hostile, but Trent Reznor later cited the record as an influence.
werk/gary-numan-telekon.listen: Listen to Remember I Was Vapour and notice the wistful atmosphere: can you hear how the song sounds like a farewell?

werk/gary-numan-the-pleasure-principle.text:
Six months after Replicas, his last record with Tubeway Army, Gary Numan released his first solo album on Beggars Banquet in September 1979. The recording took place at Marcus Music Studio in London, while Replicas was at the top of the albums chart. It became his first number one in England.

Numan left out the electric guitar entirely. Together with plenty of synthetic percussion, that gave him the most electronic and robotic sound of his career. He used Minimoog and Polymoog, and added violin and viola. The lyrics are about technology and the future. Airlane is an instrumental opening number. In Metal, an android who wants to become human sings, and Complex reached number six in England. Cars became his biggest hit, also in America and Canada. The title comes from a painting by René Magritte, which Numan recreated on the sleeve with shiny, artificial objects. He toured with an enormous show featuring neon lighting and moving pyramids.
werk/gary-numan-the-pleasure-principle.listen: Listen to Cars and notice how the song runs on synthesizers and a cool, mechanical rhythm, without an electric guitar.

werk/gary-peacock-december-poems.text:
December Poems is a solo album by the American jazz bassist Gary Peacock. He recorded it in December 1977 and it was released in 1979 on the ECM label. The Norwegian saxophonist Jan Garbarek plays on two duets, on tenor and soprano saxophone. All six pieces are by the bassist himself, from Snow Dance to Celebrations. Many titles suggest winter, such as Winterlude and A Northern Tale.

The reception was positive. AllMusic wrote that the album has a sparse and somewhat cold atmosphere, but that the bassist's virtuosity and beautiful tone come into their own in a solo setting. The DownBeat reviewer Art Lange called the record a gem.
werk/gary-peacock-december-poems.listen: Listen to Winterlude, one of the two pieces on which Jan Garbarek plays, and notice how the saxophone relates to the bass.

werk/gary-peacock-shift-in-the-wind.text:
The American jazz bassist Gary Peacock recorded Shift in the Wind in February 1980. The album was released later that year on ECM. It is a trio: Peacock plays bass, Art Lande piano and Eliot Zigmund drums. There are seven pieces on it. Three are by Peacock himself, two by Lande, and Fractions and Centers were written jointly by the three musicians.

Scott Yanow wrote for AllMusic that the interplay between these masterly musicians matters more than the compositions, and that the album rewards repeated listening. Caverns Beneath the Zoth, at just over ten minutes, is the longest piece on the record. The shortest is Fractions, at a little over five minutes.
werk/gary-peacock-shift-in-the-wind.listen: Listen to Caverns Beneath the Zoth and follow how bass, piano and drums respond to one another.

werk/gary-peacock-tales-of-another.text:
Tales of Another is an album by the bassist Gary Peacock, recorded on 2 February 1977 and released later that year on ECM. The trio with the pianist Keith Jarrett and the drummer Jack DeJohnette was the first recording by the group that later became known as Jarrett's Standards Trio. DeJohnette related that Peacock had asked the two of them for his recording session and that the producer Manfred Eicher then suggested to Jarrett that they form a trio. They decided to play standards as a springboard. They did not come together again until January 1983, for the sessions of Standards, Vol. 1, Standards, Vol. 2 and Changes.

All the pieces are by the bassist himself. He was relieved that he did not have to explain anything to the others: musically, they understood immediately what he meant. Critics praised the close interplay. The biographer Ian Carr called the record one of the classic albums of the 1970s.
werk/gary-peacock-tales-of-another.listen: Listen to Vignette and notice how bass, piano and drums respond to each other, without any of the three claiming the leading role.

werk/gary-peacock-voice-from-the-past-pa.text:
The American jazz bassist Gary Peacock recorded this album in August 1981. It was released a year later on ECM. It is a quartet with the saxophonist Jan Garbarek, the trumpeter Tomasz Stańko and the drummer Jack DeJohnette. Garbarek plays tenor and soprano saxophone. There are six pieces on it, from Voice From the Past to Ode For Tomten.

The AllMusic reviewer David R. Adler found the interplay between Peacock and DeJohnette particularly interesting, above all because it was recorded more than two years before Keith Jarrett's first standards record. He also wrote that he wished the horns sounded less tinny.
werk/gary-peacock-voice-from-the-past-pa.listen: Listen to Paradigm and follow the interplay between Peacock's bass and Jack DeJohnette's drums.

werk/gato-barbieri-chapter-one-latin-ame.text:
Gato Barbieri recorded Chapter One: Latin America in 1973 and it was released that same year on Impulse! Records. The album follows Bolivia, his previous record. The Argentinian saxophonist surrounds himself with musicians playing South American instruments: quena, Indian harp, charango, anapa, erke, siku and bombo legüero. On the fourth track Dino Saluzzi plays bandoneon.

The record has five parts. Encuentros and India are long pieces, and La China Leoncia Arreó la Correntinada Trajo Entre la Muchachada la Flor de la Juventud is made up of four parts. Robert Christgau called Barbieri a jazz musician who translates the avant-garde into something semi-popular without sounding opportunistic. AllMusic counts the record among the forgotten high points of 1970s jazz. In 1997 it appeared again in the double album Latino America.
werk/gato-barbieri-chapter-one-latin-ame.listen: Listen to Encuentros and notice how the South American wind and string instruments relate to Barbieri's tenor saxophone.

werk/gato-barbieri-fenix.text:
Fenix contains recordings from 1971 and was released on the Flying Dutchman label. Gato Barbieri, the Argentinian saxophonist and composer, plays tenor saxophone and is supported by a rich rhythm section: Lonnie Liston Smith on piano and electric piano, Ron Carter on electric bass and Lenny White on drums. Gene Golden and Naná Vasconcelos provide conga, bongo and berimbau, and on the opening track Joe Beck plays electric guitar.

The repertoire is international. Besides Tupac Amaru by Barbieri himself, there are Carnavalito, Falsa Bahiana, El Día Que Me Quieras, El Arriero and Bahia, pieces by South American composers. Robert Christgau wrote in 1971 that it was the first jazz he had enjoyed playing often since Miles Davis's In a Silent Way. AllMusic calls it an engaging album for lovers of rhythmic free jazz.
werk/gato-barbieri-fenix.listen: Listen to Carnavalito, the longest track, and notice the role of the percussion alongside the tenor saxophone.

werk/genesis-a-trick-of-the-tail.text:
At the end of 1974, the singer Peter Gabriel decided to leave Genesis. The rest of the band looked for a new frontman, but had already written an album when the music press got the news in August 1975. Recording began in October at Trident Studios in London, with David Hentschel as producer. An advertisement in Melody Maker brought about 400 replies, but no singer. In the end the drummer Phil Collins reluctantly sang Squonk, and the others felt he should do it.

The music is progressive rock, largely written by Tony Banks and Mike Rutherford. Los Endos closes the album with glances back at earlier pieces and a few lines from Supper's Ready as a salute to Gabriel. Critics were impressed that the group had survived the departure without any loss of quality. The album reached number 3 in the United Kingdom. On the tour, Bill Bruford appeared behind the drums.
werk/genesis-a-trick-of-the-tail.listen: Listen to Los Endos and notice the moments when themes from earlier pieces return. At the end, hear whether you recognise the lines from Supper's Ready.

werk/genesis-foxtrot.text:
Genesis made Foxtrot in the summer of 1972, in between concerts. After Nursery Cryme the group gained in popularity, especially in Italy and Belgium. The songs combined pieces that had already been played live, such as Watcher of the Skies and Can-Utility and the Coastliners, with new material from jam sessions. The recording at Island Studios in London went badly. The band clashed with the producer Bob Potter, among other things over the Mellotron opening of Watcher of the Skies, and the sessions were broken off. The group then continued with Dave Hitchcock.

The album contains Supper's Ready, at 23 minutes the longest piece the band had recorded. The sleeve, the last by Paul Whitehead, shows a fox in a red dress. Peter Gabriel put on that dress and a fox's head during the tour, which drew attention from the press. Foxtrot was the group's first album in the British charts, received mostly good reviews and is still praised.
werk/genesis-foxtrot.listen: Listen to Supper's Ready and notice how the piece moves on in sections, from quiet and folk-like to grand and dramatic.

werk/genesis-from-genesis-to-revelation.text:
From Genesis to Revelation, Genesis's debut, was released on 28 March 1969 on Decca. The basis was a pile of demos from 1967, recorded when the band members were still pupils at Charterhouse in Godalming. They gave the tape to Jonathan King, who gave the group its name, arranged contracts and booked studio time at Regent Sound Studios. Later Arthur Greenslade added strings to some of the songs. During the recording, John Silver replaced the drummer Chris Stewart.

The album and the singles, including Silent Sun and A Winter's Tale, flopped and received mixed to negative reviews. King felt that the young musicians still had to learn to play and kept their complicated arrangements short. In mid-1969 the group broke off contact with him. In 1974, when the band had become popular, the album did reach number 170 on the American Billboard 200.
werk/genesis-from-genesis-to-revelation.listen: Listen to Where the Sour Turns to Sweet and notice how pop-like and simple this sounds, with a string arrangement added.

werk/genesis-selling-england-by-the-poun.text:
After the tour for Foxtrot the band had little time to write new songs. Charisma gave them two to three months. Most of the music came about in an old house in Chessington and beneath a dance school in London. In August 1973 the group recorded the album at Island Studios, with John Burns as co-producer. Peter Gabriel wanted to look at Englishness in a different way. The title, a slogan from a Labour Party election manifesto, refers to the decline of English folk culture and increasing Americanisation.

The drummer Phil Collins let himself be influenced by the Mahavishnu Orchestra and played more complicated time signatures, among other places in Dancing With the Moonlit Knight. From a guitar riff by Steve Hackett grew I Know What I Like (In Your Wardrobe), the group's first British top thirty hit. The album reached third place in England. Critics and band members thought differently about it, but its reputation has grown over time.
werk/genesis-selling-england-by-the-poun.listen: In Dancing With the Moonlit Knight, listen to Phil Collins's drumming, and notice the complicated time signatures.

werk/genesis-the-lamb-lies-down-on-broad.text:
In May 1974 Genesis finished the tour for Selling England by the Pound and withdrew to Headley Grange, a large former workhouse, to write new material. The band wanted to make a double album, before it even knew what it would be about. Peter Gabriel devised the story of Rael, a rebellious youth in New York who ends up in an underworld, and wrote all the lyrics. That broke with the habit of working together. The other four therefore wrote the music mainly in jam sessions.

The record leaves behind the English fairyland of earlier work and opts for American imagery, experimental sounds and shorter songs. Critics reacted in mixed fashion, and sales lagged behind those of its predecessors. Gabriel left the band afterwards. In retrospect the album is often seen as a high point of progressive rock.
werk/genesis-the-lamb-lies-down-on-broad.listen: Listen to The Carpet Crawlers and notice how quiet and strange this piece sounds, like a fragment from Rael's dream story.

werk/genesis-trespass.text:
Trespass was released on 23 October 1970 on Charisma Records and is the last album with the guitarist Anthony Phillips and the only one with the drummer John Mayhew. In the preceding months the band wrote most of the material at Christmas Cottage in Surrey and played a lot live. In July 1970 it recorded the album at Trident Studios in London, with John Anthony as producer and engineer.

The music opts for folk-like progressive rock instead of the pop sound of the debut. Dusk is light and acoustic, with several twelve-string guitars, while The Knife is heavier and a favourite on stage. Shortly after the recording Phillips left, which almost caused the group to break up. The album had little success and received mixed reviews, but did well in Belgium.
werk/genesis-trespass.listen: Listen to Dusk and notice the twelve-string guitars, which here do not stay in the background but carry the melody themselves.

werk/george-baker-selection-little-green.text: In 1969 the George Baker Selection, from the Zaanstreek region, had a hit with Little Green Bag, which was also a hit in America in 1970. The singer Hans Bouwens performed as George Baker. The song begins with a famous bass line. In 1992 the director Quentin Tarantino used it in the film Reservoir Dogs, and so a new generation heard it. Dutch pop music crossed the border in those years mainly in English.
werk/george-baker-selection-little-green.listen: Listen to the bass line and the drums at the start: a few bars that later became famous in an American film.

werk/george-benson-shape-of-things-to-co.text:
After four years and three different labels, George Benson signed with A&M/CTI in 1968. He had to take the place of Wes Montgomery, the label's star, who had died earlier that year. For this first album, producer Creed Taylor brought in all of the label's heavyweights: the arranger Don Sebesky, the engineer Rudy Van Gelder and guests such as Herbie Hancock and Ron Carter.

It is Benson's fifth studio album and the first that Taylor produced. He would continue to do so until 1976. The repertoire consists largely of covers of artists as different as Aretha Franklin, the Monkees and Glenn Miller. In addition there are two originals and arrangements of film music.
werk/george-benson-shape-of-things-to-co.listen: Listen to Last Train to Clarksville and notice how a Monkees pop song is given a jazz treatment here.

werk/george-benson-the-george-benson-coo.text:
The George Benson Cookbook is the guitarist George Benson's third studio album and his second under the producer John Hammond. His quartet is modelled on that of Jack McDuff, with the baritone saxophonist Ronnie Cuber, the organist Lonnie Smith and the drummer Jimmy Lovelace or Marion Booker. On some pieces the trombonist Bennie Green and the percussionist Pucho also play.

Cuber's baritone sax gives the group a richer, denser sound than McDuff with his tenor sax. The whole is soul jazz, with an emphasis on rhythm. According to the Hard Bop Homepage, the trombone and percussion gave a bop feel that appealed to jazz lovers and critics. On All of Me Benson also sings himself.
werk/george-benson-the-george-benson-coo.listen: Listen to All of Me and notice Benson's singing, alongside his guitar playing.

werk/george-clinton-computer-games.text:
Computer Games came out on 5 November 1982 on Capitol Records. Formally it is George Clinton's first solo record, but almost the same musicians played on it as on recent Parliament and Funkadelic records, the groups he had disbanded in 1981. The album came about after a period of financial and personal problems. According to Trouser Press, the title nods to the emerging techno-funk: Clinton did not reject the new technology but applied it in his own way.

Loopzilla reached the top twenty of the R&B chart, and then Atomic Dog went to number 1 on the same chart. The record made Clinton briefly popular again, before P-Funk ran into new legal problems and little support from the label in the mid-1980s. Slant Magazine placed the album at number 97 among the best albums of the 1980s.
werk/george-clinton-computer-games.listen: Listen to Atomic Dog and notice what role the electronic sounds play alongside the funk rhythm.

werk/george-clinton-you-shouldn-t-nuf-bi.text:
You Shouldn't-Nuf Bit Fish is George Clinton's second solo album, released in 1983 by Capitol Records. Clinton produced it himself. He made Quickie together with Junie Morrison, and Last Dance and the title song with Garry Shider. The record builds on the R&B and dance style of his debut Computer Games of 1982. The musicians include Bootsy Collins, Bernie Worrell, Maceo Parker and Fred Wesley.

In addition, the album contains elements of rock and sounds more mainstream. Nubian Nut reached fifteenth place on the Hot Soul Songs chart, Last Dance twenty-sixth. The album itself reached number 18 on the Top Soul Albums chart. The P-Funk tour of 1984 centred mainly on the songs from this record.
werk/george-clinton-you-shouldn-t-nuf-bi.listen: Listen to Nubian Nut, the album's biggest soul hit, and notice how funk here seeks its way towards a mainstream sound.

werk/george-gershwin-swanee.text: George Gershwin began as a teenager as a song plugger for a publisher in Tin Pan Alley: he played new songs to customers and performers. In 1919 he wrote Swanee, with the lyricist Irving Caesar. When the famous singer Al Jolson recorded it in 1920, it became Gershwin's first big hit, with an estimated two million records sold. Later Gershwin wrote Rhapsody in Blue and the opera Porgy and Bess.
werk/george-gershwin-swanee.listen: Hear how Al Jolson sings with big flourishes, as in the theatre, with an orchestra that follows the rhythm of ragtime.

werk/george-harrison-all-things-must-pas.text:
After the break-up of the Beatles in April 1970, George Harrison began work on what he called his first real solo album. He had for years been saving up songs that were not used with the Beatles. In the meantime he had spent time with Bob Dylan, The Band, Delaney & Bonnie and Billy Preston. Recording began in May 1970 at EMI Studios in London, with, among others, Eric Clapton, Ringo Starr, Gary Wright and Klaus Voormann. Phil Spector was co-producer.

Spector gave the music his Wall of Sound: according to Rolling Stone it sounded like mountain peaks and wide horizons. Here the recognisable slide guitar is heard for the first time, with the spiritual themes that return in his later work. My Sweet Lord and What Is Life became hits; Isn't It a Pity and the title track had previously been left on the shelf. The album was released as a triple album, with informal jams on the third disc, and is often regarded as the best solo album by an ex-Beatle.
werk/george-harrison-all-things-must-pas.listen: In My Sweet Lord, listen to the slide guitar and notice how it defines the sound of the song.

werk/george-harrison-dark-horse.text:
Dark Horse came out in December 1974 on Apple Records, as the successor to Living in the Material World. George Harrison wrote and recorded the album in a turbulent period. His marriage to Pattie Boyd was breaking down, he drank heavily and he directed his energy mainly at his new label Dark Horse Records, with Ravi Shankar and the group Splinter. Many guest musicians played on it, among them Ringo Starr, Billy Preston and Ron Wood.

The songs are about the end of his marriage and about doubt. In So Sad he writes about the break-up, and in Bye Bye Love he rewrote the lyrics of the Everly Brothers. The sound moves towards funk and soul, especially in Māya Love and Far East Man. Ding Dong, Ding Dong and Dark Horse became singles. Most critics were negative at the time, partly because of the controversial tour with Shankar.
werk/george-harrison-dark-horse.listen: Listen to Hari's on Tour (Express). Notice the slide guitar, which plays the leading role in this rare instrumental piece.

werk/george-michael-faith.text:
Faith is The Cure's third studio album and came out on 17 April 1981 on Fiction Records. It is the first record after the departure of the keyboard player Matthieu Hartley, who disagreed with the musical direction. The band first recorded in September 1980 at Morgan Studios, but the recordings sounded too dull to Robert Smith. The band then tried more studios, including Abbey Road. Many songs came about in the studio. All Cats Are Grey and The Drowning Man were inspired by the Gormenghast novels of Mervyn Peake.

The record continues the gloomy line of Seventeen Seconds. The British press was divided: Melody Maker praised the richness and hidden strength, while other critics thought it sounded too much like Pink Floyd. Later AllMusic called it a depressing but also underrated and beautiful record. In 2010 Fact placed it among the twenty best gothic records ever.
werk/george-michael-faith.listen: Listen to All Cats Are Grey and notice the keyboards and piano, where in this song no guitar is heard.

werk/george-shearing-bossa-nova.text:
After the tour for Doolittle, three of the Pixies moved from Boston to Los Angeles in January 1990, where they wanted to record the new album. The bassist Kim Deal followed later. They lived in the same apartment complex as the producer Gil Norton. The recording at Cherokee Studios in February ground to a halt: the mixing desk picked up pirate radio stations and guitar amplifiers gave off an enormous hum. Through the producer Rick Rubin the band found another studio, Master Control.

Unlike before, the members wrote many songs only in the studio. The band rehearsed for only two weeks, and Black Francis wrote some lyrics just before he sang them. Velouria and Dig for Fire became singles. According to the British press, the production lay close to the raw sound of Surfer Rosa, with the strong melodies of Doolittle. Rolling Stone called it a straightforward rock album by the band's standards. In the United Kingdom it reached third place.
werk/george-shearing-bossa-nova.listen: In Velouria, listen to the way the melody and the raw guitars alternate.

werk/george-shearing-old-gold-and-ivory.text:
Old Gold and Ivory is an album by the pianist George Shearing, accompanied by his quintet and a string orchestra conducted by Milt Raskin. The repertoire comes from classical music. Shearing plays, among others, Ritual Fire Dance by Manuel de Falla, a prelude by Chopin, the theme from Scheherazade by Rimsky-Korsakov, None But the Lonely Heart by Tchaikovsky and Pavane by Fauré. There are also pieces by Brahms, Grieg, Lecuona, Cyril Scott and Percy Grainger.

Shearing wrote the arrangements for strings, horns and woodwinds himself. The horn and woodwind players are not known. Reactions varied. Billboard wrote in April 1964 that the result was smooth, uncomplicated and creatively exciting. Scott Yanow of AllMusic found the performances well played and pleasant, but never rising above the level of sleepy background music.
werk/george-shearing-old-gold-and-ivory.listen: In Ritual Fire Dance, listen to how Shearing plays a classical piece with quintet and strings, and notice how much of the original music remains recognisable.

werk/george-shearing-the-shearing-touch.text:
The Shearing Touch is a 1960 album by George Shearing's quintet with orchestra, arranged by Billy May. It contains twelve well-known pieces, such as Autumn Nocturne, Misty, Autumn Leaves, Honeysuckle Rose and One O'Clock Jump. Most last only two to three minutes.

The AllMusic reviewer pointed to unusual time signatures, to classical techniques and to the use of light pop melodies, accents and subtle rhythms. The pianist leads the quintet and May wrote the arrangements. The source tells us no more about how this album came about. The combination of a jazz quintet with orchestra gives the familiar songs a different colour from their usual versions.
werk/george-shearing-the-shearing-touch.listen: Listen to Autumn Leaves and notice how the quintet and the orchestra together carry the familiar melody.

werk/gerry-mulligan-mulligan-meets-monk.text:
Mulligan Meets Monk is a studio album by the baritone saxophonist Gerry Mulligan and the pianist Thelonious Monk, originally released in 1957 on Riverside Records. Orrin Keepnews was the producer and also wrote the liner notes. The quartet was completed by the bassist Wilbur Ware and the drummer Shadow Wilson.

The repertoire consists of six pieces: standards such as Round Midnight and Sweet and Lovely, alongside pieces by Monk such as Rhythm-a-Ning, Straight, No Chaser and I Mean You. Decidedly is by Mulligan himself. The album has been reissued many times and came out on CD in 1987 with extra alternate takes from the same session.
werk/gerry-mulligan-mulligan-meets-monk.listen: Listen to Round Midnight and notice how baritone saxophone and piano take turns drawing the attention to themselves.

werk/gerry-mulligan-two-of-a-mind.text:
The alto saxophonist Paul Desmond and the baritone saxophonist Gerry Mulligan recorded this album in 1962 for RCA Victor, at Webster Hall and RCA Studio A in New York. It is their second record in a quartet without piano. The first, Blues in Time, was recorded in 1957. On bass were John Beal, Joe Benjamin and Wendell Marshall, on drums Connie Kay, Mel Lewis and Ed Shaughnessy.

The title song is a contrafact of Look for the Silver Lining. There are also standards such as All the Things You Are, Stardust, The Way You Look Tonight and Out of Nowhere, and Mulligan's Blight of the Fumble Bee. Allmusic gave the album four and a half stars. According to that review, both saxophonists have a recognisably light sound, strong humour and the ability to improvise melodically, and their interplay is consistently delightful.
werk/gerry-mulligan-two-of-a-mind.listen: Listen to Stardust, at over eight minutes the longest piece on the original record, and notice how alto and baritone saxophone keep each other in balance without a piano.

werk/gers-pardoel-ik-neem-je-mee.text: On 17 October 2011, Ik neem je mee by the Nijmegen rapper Gers Pardoel was released. The cheerful love song spent a total of six weeks at number 1 in the Top 40. In 2012 it became the most successful Dutch-language hit ever in the Top 40, a record that was not broken until 2023. Rap in one's own language now belonged entirely in the ordinary hit parade.
werk/gers-pardoel-ik-neem-je-mee.listen: Hear how Gers raps and sings at the same time, over a sunny, simple guitar beat.

werk/gil-evans-gil-evans-en-ten.text:
Gil Evans & Ten was released in 1957 on the Prestige label and is the first album as bandleader by the pianist, conductor, arranger and composer Gil Evans. It also came out under the titles Big Stuff and Gil Evans + Ten. The recording took place in September and October 1957.

The programme consists of arrangements of five standards and one original composition, Jambangle, with, among others, Steve Lacy, Lee Konitz, Jimmy Cleveland and Paul Chambers. The arranger uses the voices of this unusual combination of musicians in an inventive way. According to AllMusic, it is a good introduction to his work, with pieces ranging from Lead Belly to Leonard Bernstein. The Penguin Guide to Jazz calls it a record that stands in the shadow of later sessions, but that offers much to enjoy.
werk/gil-evans-gil-evans-en-ten.listen: Listen to Big Stuff and notice how the different horns give the arrangement their own colour.
